newsitem.title: USA: Clinton says White House not for sale to donors.
newsitem.headline: Clinton says White House not for sale to donors.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday rejected any suggestion he had induced people to donate campaign funds by offering overnight stays at the White House, saying: "The Lincoln Bedroom was never sold."
"That was one more false story we have had to endure, and the facts will show what the truth is," Clinton told reporters when asked about it after a speech on his anti-drug policy.

The White House said it would release a list of those invited to stay overnight as Clinton's guests in an apparent effort to counter news reports suggesting such invitations may have been an inducement to campaign donors.

"Later today we're going to release ... the numbers of people who stayed at the White House in the last four years and you will see that the people who worked for me and helped to raise funds for me were a small percentage of the total number of people who stayed at the White House," Clinton said.

The president and his Democratic Party have become ensnarled in disclosures that the White House and the party engaged in questionable money-raising practices during the 1996 presidential and congressional election campaigns.
Clinton defended the inclusion of financial backers among those invited to sleep at the White House, portraying it as an effort to re-establish contact with "estranged" contributors.

"There's a document there that points out that in early 1995 a lot of the people that helped me get elected president in 1992 thought that they had gotten estranged, in effect, from me -- that we had not kept in touch with them," he said.
Clinton said former campaign fund-raiser Terry McAuliffe had suggested ways to re-establish contact, and said he thought it was a good idea.

"In addition to that ... I wanted to ask some of my friends who had helped me when I got elected president that I hadn't been in touch with to come to the White House and spend the night with me," he said. "They were my friends and I was proud to have them here I did not have any strangers here. The Lincoln Bedroom was never sold."
The White House said in a statement by press spokesman Mike McCurry that "in no case was staying overnight at the White House contingent upon a political contribution."

The documents being released belong to former White House deputy chief of staff Harold Ickes and have been given to a congressional committee investigating fundraising practices during last year's election.

The Democratic National Committee, leadership group of the president's party, has returned over $1.4 million in questionable donations and party sources said it expects to return more once an internal audit of donors is completed.
The McCurry statement said the documents would also detail Clinton's attendance at White House coffee meetings organised by the party and his re-election campaign, and added:

"No solicitation of funds was made at these coffees. As far as we are aware, no one was required to make a contribution, or to commit to do so, in order to attend these White House events. If anyone raising money for the campaign asked for such commitments, they were acting contrary to White House and DNC guidelines."

Clinton last week apologised for the fund-raising problems in the campaign that led to his re-election, saying he could not "explain or defend" the party's failure to check all the contributions that came in to ensure that they were legal.
He has been calling for campaign finance reform but his appeal appears to have met little enthusiasm within Congress, where all legislators were elected under the current system.
